title: Supply and demand ↔ tomatoes at the market

learning.goal: See how the price settles where the crates that arrived (supply) meet what buyers are willing to pay (demand), and why more crates mean a lower price.
learning.question: A late frost ruins half of the tomato fields near town. Next Saturday, what happens to the price of a crate at the market, and why?
learning.answer: Fewer crates arrive, so the supply line moves to the left. With the same buyers wanting tomatoes, the seller can sell every crate at a higher price: the meeting point slides up along the demand curve. Some buyers decide tomatoes are too expensive and buy fewer or none.
learning.caveat: The prices are made up to keep the numbers simple, and the demand curve is drawn as a straight line. Supply is fixed here because the crates are already at the market and tomatoes spoil in a day or two; over a season, farmers react to prices by planting more or less. Demand can move too: a heatwave or a pasta-sauce trend shifts the whole blue line.

steps.text: Why are tomatoes cheap some Saturdays?
steps.say: Same market, same tomatoes. So why is a crate expensive one Saturday and cheap the next?

steps.text: How much for a crate of tomatoes?
steps.say: Sam asks the price. Rosa's answer depends on how many crates the truck brought this morning.

steps.text: Only {crates} crates came in, and everyone wants them. ${price:0} a crate!
{crates} crates today, a normal day. ${price:0} a crate.
{crates} crates, and they go soft by tonight! ${price:0} a crate, please buy!

steps.say: Few crates: Rosa can ask a lot, someone will pay. Many crates: she has to cut the price before they spoil.
Put it on a graph. The blue line is demand: the cheaper the crate, the more crates buyers take.
The red line is supply: today it is simply the crates on the truck, whatever the price.
Where the lines cross is the price that sells every crate: the market price.
Move the crates. More crates push the red line right and the price slides down the blue line.

steps.text: same buyers + more crates = lower price
steps.say: Fewer crates, the opposite: buyers compete and the price climbs.
